Hinduism is the family of religious traditions that grew up in India, today followed by more than a billion people, most of them in India and Nepal. It has no single founder, creed or church. What holds it together is a shared respect for the Vedas, ideas of dharma (right order and duty), karma and rebirth, and a vast body of gods, stories and rituals.

Its oldest roots lie in the religion of the Vedic period. The Rigveda, composed around 1500 to 1200 BCE, holds hymns to gods of fire, storm and sky, sung at sacrifices led by Brahmin priests. The Upanishads then turned inward, teaching that the self, atman, is one with brahman, the ground of all being, and that release from rebirth, moksha, is the highest goal.

Over the next thousand years came most of what Hindus practise today:

  • the epics Mahabharata, with the Bhagavad Gita, and Ramayana;
  • devotion to great gods, above all Vishnu and his avatars Rama and Krishna, Shiva, and the Goddess;
  • temple worship, from the Gupta age on, rising to temples such as Khajuraho;
  • the social order of varna and the caste system.

Thinkers such as Adi Shankara gave it system. Bhakti poets, among them Kabir, preached love of God over ritual and caste. Indian traders and priests carried Hindu ideas to Southeast Asia, where the Yupa inscriptions of Kutai are among the earliest traces. In the 1800s reformers such as Vivekananda and the Ramakrishna Mission presented Hinduism to the world as one religion.
